retro.headline: Sewer Commission voted to send a delinquent Sunny Hill Road account to the tax collector with no payment plan.
retro.summary: The commission voted to refer a long-delinquent sewer account to the tax collector for tax lien and decline a payment plan. It also heard updates on a contract RFR and second-quarter billing, and began discussing raising the sewer demand fee and interest rate, held for a later meeting with a public hearing required. It voted to move the December 29 meeting to January 12.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted to send the balance on a delinquent Sunny Hill Road account to the tax collector for a tax lien and not to offer a payment plan.
The DPW director's suggested monthly payment plan, covering most of a year's bill with any remainder going on the tax lien, was rejected.
The commission began discussing a higher sewer demand fee and interest rate; counsel said the legal maximum rate is above the current one. It was held for a later meeting.
A request for responses for contractor services went out, with bids due in mid-November, to place a contractor before the current contract expires.
The commission voted to move the December 29 Zoom meeting to January 12.

why_it_matters: Sewer fees are billed to property owners, and an account left unpaid can be added to the property's tax bill as a lien, so this vote shows how the town collects overdue sewer charges.
Any change to the demand fee or interest rate would change what sewer users are billed, and the commission said it needs a public hearing with newspaper notice first.
watch_next: Demand fee and interest rate discussion returns at a meeting when Chip is present, after the business manager gathers comparable towns' fees; a public hearing is required to change the regulation.
Next meetings: Nov 10 (hybrid at DPW), Nov 24 (Zoom), Dec 8 (hybrid), then Jan 12, 2027.

retro.headline: Select Board recommended disapproval of the special ed reserve transfer and deferred budget and track articles for the Nov 17 special town meeting.
retro.summary: The board reviewed the draft special town meeting warrant, voting on recommendations for several articles and deferring others pending certified free cash. It also discussed a draft flag policy, whether to draft a special education reserve fund policy (referred back to the school committee), and heard the town manager's report including a delay in free cash certification.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-1 to recommend disapproval of Article 4, a transfer from free cash to the special education reserve fund.
The board deferred Articles 2 and 3, and separately Article 9 (track and field engineering), to be voted on after the town knows its certified free cash.
The board recommended approval of Articles 1, 5 and 6, took no position 4-1 on the non-binding straw polls in Articles 7 and 8, and approved the warrant.
A motion to have the town manager draft a special education reserve fund policy was withdrawn; the matter goes to the school committee chair for their agenda first.
The town manager reported that year-end close is slow and free cash may not be certified in time for the special town meeting.

why_it_matters: Several warrant articles depend on free cash, and until it is certified the board cannot finalize recommendations on them, so voters at the special town meeting may be asked to act on items the board has not yet weighed in on.

Article 4 would move money from free cash into a special education reserve, a fund that cushions the town budget, which is mostly taxes, against unplanned placement costs, and the board's recommendation against it is advisory only; Town Meeting makes the decision.
watch_next: Nov 17: the board meets at 6:30, before the special town meeting, to vote on the deferred articles, then Town Meeting votes on the warrant.
Nov 10: Select Board meeting, partly a workshop on the draft flag policy.

retro.headline: Finance Committee heard the stormwater utility, library, special education reserve and track articles; no article votes.
retro.summary: At a public hearing on the November 17 special town meeting warrant, the finance director said free cash likely won't be certified by then. Members heard the stormwater utility presentation and went through the articles. Members voiced reservations about the stormwater utility, funding the special education reserve, and the track engineering funding source. Only procedural votes were taken.

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee held a public hearing on the November 17 special town meeting warrant and took no votes on any article.

Members heard the stormwater utility presentation, including the fee structure and the operating budget, and discussed Article 8.
Members voiced reservations about the stormwater utility, the special education reserve transfer and the funding source for track engineering.

retro.headline: Trust Fund Commission voted unanimously to adopt nine governing documents, including the resident guide, operational manual and investment policy.
retro.summary: The chair walked through the new resident guide for applying to town trust funds, the operational manual and application forms. The two members present then adopted all nine documents in one motion. The chair also reported on the Select Board declining the warrant article, the unanswered charter question, the pending Attorney General review and a dispute with the school department over trust fund records.

what_happened.line: The Trust Fund Commission voted unanimously, by voice vote of the two members present, to adopt nine governing documents in a single motion.
The nine include the resident guide, operational manual, investment policy statement, risk mitigation policy, application forms and a resident checklist.
The chair reported the trust fund matter will not go into the special town meeting warrant; the advertisement is still to be drafted and ratified.
The commission is still waiting on pre-filing form language from the town manager before a vote and a roughly six-week Attorney General review.
The school department records dispute was not resolved; the next step is asking the Select Board to enforce the request, with discussion set for the next meeting.

why_it_matters: The adopted resident guide and forms set out how residents apply for town trust fund money, including income eligibility, savings expectations and payment directly to businesses.
With the warrant article off the special town meeting, any change to how trust funds are governed or invested waits on the Attorney General review and a later vote.
watch_next: Next meeting November 11, 2026: the school department letter, the risk management policy review and the September 10 and December 18 minutes.
The vote on the pre-filing form once the town manager supplies the language, then the Attorney General review.

retro.headline: Committee declined to change float rules for non-LHS students; FY28 capital plan led by turf/track safety fix, no votes on priorities.
retro.summary: The committee approved minutes, line item transfers, two donations and the cafeteria workers contract. It declined to pursue a policy letting non-LHS students join homecoming float, and reviewed current and FY28-FY33 capital projects, with the turf, track and retaining wall failure the top priority. It then moved to executive session on an open meeting law complaint.

what_happened.line: The School Committee ratified the cafeteria workers contract on a roll call vote that passed unanimously.
The committee voted to leave float participation as is, so non-LHS students stay under existing LHS practice; the vote result was not audible and no policy work was referred.
Members reviewed the FY28 to FY33 capital plan, with the turf, track and retaining wall failure the top priority, but took no vote on priorities.
The committee accepted line item transfers and two donations, one for Best Buddies and one of jerseys for the unified basketball team.
The facilities director was asked to add the primary school roof to the capital plan, and members want the primary boilers moved up.

why_it_matters: The capital plan sets which school building and field projects compete for a limited share of town capital money, and the turf and track work is likely to reach residents as a debt exclusion vote, which would raise tax bills.
The schools usually receive only a fraction of what they request, so items such as the roof and boilers may be delayed or left unfunded until the plan is voted.
watch_next: A later committee vote on capital priorities, which was not taken at this meeting.
The special town meeting warrant article on the turf field, mentioned in the chair's report.

retro.headline: Parks Commission left field fees unchanged until the FY28 maintenance contract is known, and tabled Wallace Park lights.
retro.summary: The commission voted to partner with the LBA on a May 2027 spring vendor fair, reviewed a spreadsheet of FY26 field costs, and discussed field usage fees without changing them. It also took up the lack of a written agreement with the schools for facility use, the rec director's funding, and proposed Wallace Park lights. It approved overdue April minutes and tabled the lights until the revolving fund balance is confirmed.

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission made no change to field user fees this year and will revisit them once the FY28 maintenance contract costs are known.
Wallace Park lights were tabled until the town confirms the revolving fund balance after the rec director's salary is paid from it.
The commission voted to partner with the LBA on a spring vendor fair on May 22, 2027; the minutes record the vote tally as not audible.
Members aim to reach a consensus on fees by January, with a discussion in December and a vote in January.
Two members will meet town staff or the town manager to draft a facilities agreement with the schools before approaching the superintendent's office.

why_it_matters: Youth leagues' per-player fees stay as they are for now, while the minutes show baseball fees totalling far less than the infield maintenance contract lines for its fields, so the question of who pays for field upkeep stays open into the winter.
The rec director's salary is paid from the same parks revolving fund that would pay for Wallace Park lights, so a new park amenity competes with a staff position for one pot of money.
Schools and town fields are used without a written agreement, so who may use them and who pays for upkeep rests on nothing in writing until one is drafted.
watch_next: A fee discussion at the December meeting, held in early December rather than the week before Thanksgiving, and a fee vote in January.
The town's confirmation of the parks revolving fund balance, which the commission needs before it takes up Wallace Park lights again.

retro.headline: Water commissioners allowed C909 plastic pipe on two projects and backed applying for a PFAS planning grant.
retro.summary: The board allowed plastic C909 water main for the Round Road and Shirley Road projects, with the superintendent reviewing plans, and plastic service lines with tracer wire. It heard a long debate on a commissioner's PFAS blending proposal versus building a treatment plant, and backed applying for the emerging contaminants grant. It also reviewed a customer collections complaint, a water-purchase option from neighboring towns, and set November meeting dates.

what_happened.line: The Water District board allowed plastic C909 water main for the Round Road and Shirley Road projects, with the superintendent reviewing plans.
The board allowed plastic service lines on the Round Road project if tracer wire is installed.
The board approved the engineer applying for the emerging contaminants grant, going for the larger figure that includes Hickory Hills.
A long discussion compared a commissioner's PFAS blending proposal with building a treatment plant; no resolution was reached.
The board moved its November meetings to the 4th and 18th, and agreed to waive the school's finance charges if the bills are paid.

why_it_matters: The pipe material and the PFAS path (blending or a treatment plant) shape what water customers will be asked to pay for, and the treatment decision is still open.
The grant covers planning and design only, so it does not by itself fund a plant; construction would still need a funding vote.
watch_next: Questions for the state regulator are to be drafted and circulated before the Wednesday meeting.
November meetings are set for the 4th and 18th.

retro.headline: Conservation Commission approved several wetland filings, a revised Cowry ADA trail plan advanced, and $950 Hollis Road electrical work was approved.
retro.summary: The commission heard a run of wetlands hearings, approving or issuing negative determinations on most, with conditions, and continuing others. It reviewed a revised ADA trail and parking plan at the Cowry Nature Center and heard concerns from a resident about the Unitil substation project. It also adopted the 2027 meeting schedule and approved an electrician quote for the Hollis Road house.

watch_next: Continued filings return November 4, 2026 (Cowry Nature Center, 143 Island Road, 386 Sunset Lane).
404 Page Street and the 1168 Mass Ave rear enforcement matter return November 18, 2026.

what_happened.line: The commission approved the Unitil substation notice of intent with conditions, including removal and revegetation of the former substation, 5-0.
The commission approved a negative determination with conditions for 392 Sunset Lane, and approved a septic replacement at 134 Peninsula Drive with an added planting condition, both 5-0.
After a first vote failed, the commission rescinded it and approved the 134 Crawford Street project change with a fence and boulders, 5-0.
The Cowry Nature Center ADA trail and parking plan was sent to the planning board and the notice of intent continued; the grant cannot be extended.
The commission approved the 2027 meeting schedule and an amount as heard electrician quote for the Hollis Road house, both 5-0.

why_it_matters: Approvals on the Unitil substation, septic and retaining-wall filings set the conditions that shape work near wetlands and water in Lunenburg.
The Cowry trail project is grant-funded and the grant cannot be extended, so delays in review risk the funding for an accessible trail on town conservation land.
Hollis Road house spending, a proposed caretaker position for Town Meeting and a stormwater fee question touch town property costs and possibly a future fee or tax vote.

retro.headline: Board put the track and field engineering article on the special town meeting warrant and rejected the park design article.
retro.summary: The board approved a liquor license for Kiku with a prorated fee, heard a report on selling or leasing the Brooks House, and held a joint session with the Stormwater Task Force on a utility fee versus the operating budget. It heard the superintendent on the failing track and field retaining wall, then finalized the special town meeting warrant. Track and field and the stormwater advisory were included, the accessibility/park design article failed, and the trust fund continuity bylaw failed.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to place the middle high school track and field engineering article on the special town meeting warrant.
The board voted 0-5 on the accessibility and park design article, which was moved so it could be voted down, and it did not go on the warrant.
The advisory article on stormwater funding mechanisms passed 4-1, and the trust fund continuity article failed 0-5.
The board approved the Kiku liquor license unanimously with the annual fee cut to one quarter for the rest of the calendar year.
In a joint session, the Stormwater Task Force and the board discussed a utility fee versus the operating budget; the track article was later moved to last on the warrant.

why_it_matters: Voters at the special town meeting will be asked to act on design and engineering for the track and field retaining wall, which could lead to a later construction request and tax impact.
The stormwater advisory article asks voters to weigh a dedicated utility fee against paying through the operating budget, which is funded mostly by taxes.
watch_next: October 27 Select Board meeting, where the board will make its recommendations on all special town meeting warrant articles.
The November 3 election, whose warrant the board approved, and the special town meeting warrant as finalized.

retro.headline: Personnel Committee dropped the two-of-three voting change and began shaping a warrant article on job-description review and a class and comp study.
retro.summary: The committee discussed two possible warrant articles for town meeting: letting job descriptions with no changes within a set period skip committee review, and funding a town-wide classification and compensation study. After the town's counsel-style clarification on quorum and voting, members agreed to drop the proposal to change the voting threshold. They also planned a SharePoint-based procedures handbook and were reminded not to deliberate in a shared document outside a public meeting. No formal votes other than adjournment were taken.

what_happened.line: The Personnel Committee agreed to drop the proposal to change the voting and quorum threshold from its list of warrant items.
Members began shaping a warrant article on job-description review, including letting descriptions with no changes within a set period skip committee review.
Members said a town-wide classification and compensation study would need town meeting approval, though bids can be gathered beforehand.
An action item was set to email the HR director and town manager about the study's scope and who runs the bidding; a workshop with HR was also favored.
Members will send questions or markups to the chair individually, not comment in a shared document, to stay within open meeting law.

why_it_matters: A warrant article funding a classification and compensation study would be a town meeting vote residents are asked to take, and it bears on how town jobs are graded and paid.
The job-description change would alter how often committee review happens, which affects how openly changes to town positions get seen.
watch_next: Replies from the HR director and town manager on the study's scope and who runs the bidding.
The committee's draft warrant articles on job-description review and the study, before town meeting.

retro.headline: Stormwater task force reworked its slide deck to present neutral funding choices for the town's MS4 compliance to Select Board and FinCom.
retro.summary: The task force reviewed the stormwater presentation slide by slide ahead of the Select Board and Finance Committee sessions. Members agreed to retitle it around funding mechanisms, drop the tiered fee structure, add an operating-budget-versus-utility comparison, and reconcile revenue and impervious-area figures. One member showed an analysis of fee impact on commercial and residential properties. Next meeting set for the 29th on Zoom.

what_happened.line: The task force agreed to retitle its stormwater deck around funding mechanisms for MS4 compliance, rather than assuming a utility.
Members voted on nothing but agreed to drop the tiered fee structure and keep only the equivalent-residential-unit example, with example fees made consistent.
The deck will present the operating budget first, then a utility, then a side-by-side comparison, and the straw poll will ask which funding mechanism is preferred.
One member was assigned to reconcile the revenue and impervious-area figures before the Select Board and Finance Committee sessions, which will use the same deck.
The chair will recuse from the Select Board on the stormwater article, sit with the task force and not vote on the recommendation.

why_it_matters: How the town pays for stormwater compliance could land on a tax bill through the operating budget, or on a separate fee, and the task force is shaping the choice residents will be shown.
Funding from the operating budget beyond the current stormwater line would mean cuts elsewhere or an override vote, while a utility fee would be billed by property rather than raised through taxes.
watch_next: Revised deck due about end of day tomorrow, with Finance Committee materials by end of day Monday.
Next task force meeting on the 29th at 7 on Zoom.

retro.headline: ZBA voted to grant a variance letting a modular food pantry building be placed at 30 School Street.
retro.summary: The board heard the planning director preview four 2027 zoning amendments, then held a variance hearing for a one-story manufactured building to house the Lunenburg food pantry in the village center district. what_happened.line: The Zoning Board of Appeals voted to grant a variance for a one-story modular building to house the Lunenburg food pantry at 30 School Street.
The board also voted by voice to waive the application fees for the food pantry.

A member offered to arrange a talk with the Parks Commission about the back of Wallace Park as an alternative site if other options fail.
The planning director previewed four 2027 zoning amendments and asked boards for comments by the end of November.

why_it_matters: The decision lets the food pantry put a temporary building in the village center, with the site still subject to a license being negotiated with the town and a duty to restore the land when it leaves.

watch_next: Comments on the draft 2027 zoning amendments are due to the planning director by the end of November.
The pantry's license with the town for the 30 School Street site, still under negotiation, and the appeal window the chair read after the decision.

retro.headline: Sewer Commission approved moving money into the connection fees line to pay Leominster's per-connection charges.
retro.summary: The Sewer Commission met briefly and voted a transfer into the sewer connection fees line, which was exhausted by Leominster connection charges. It also heard updates on a property's connection payment, the pump station service contract renewal, and a possible sewer extension for a property up for sale.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission voted to pass a transfer from the capital plan into the sewer connection fees line to pay Leominster's per-connection charges.
The business manager said the connection fees line is the only one with room left, and it has been budgeted low while each Leominster connection carries a fixed charge.
The business manager said the line needs to be increased next year, and that fees owed to Leominster and Fitchburg are mounting.
A customer at the 786 to 796 property replaced bounced checks with a bank check, and the funds were received, clearing the building commissioner's hold.
The pump station service contract wording has cleared counsel and sits with procurement; talks with town counsel on customers in arrears are expected within a couple of weeks.

why_it_matters: Connection charges to Leominster and Fitchburg are paid through a budget line that ran out early, so the sewer budget next year will likely need a larger connection fees line, or the same mid-year transfer again.
Sewer connection fees are passed through to customers, and unpaid balances are being taken up with town counsel, which bears on what sewer ratepayers owe and how arrears are handled.
watch_next: Next meetings: Oct 27 (Zoom), Nov 10 (hybrid), Nov 24 (Zoom) and Dec 8 (hybrid at the DPW), all at 6 p.m.
Discussion with town counsel on charges and customers in arrears, expected within a couple of weeks.

retro.headline: Council on Aging sent a member's seven bylaw-change proposals to a four-member subcommittee and backed an architect study and emergency shower.
retro.summary: The meeting covered a long member presentation proposing seven changes to the board's policies and procedures, which drew objections about its scope and its lack of advance notice and was sent to a subcommittee. The board also heard about the assessor's new office hours at the senior center after an elevator mishap at the Ritter building, and voted to pursue an architect study for a building expansion and a shower for emergency sheltering. Updates on the formula grant, parking lot, events, trips and the director's report rounded out the agenda.

what_happened.line: The Council on Aging voted to add an architect study of a building expansion to its budget request, and to look at adding a shower so the center can serve as an emergency facility.
A second voice vote supported looking at a shower in the bathroom so the senior center could serve as an emergency facility.
A member's presentation proposing seven changes to the board's policies and procedures was tabled, and a four-member subcommittee was formed to collect recommendations.
The expansion and shower requests will go through the capital request process via the facilities head, and the director said the formula grant could possibly fund the architect study.
The board heard that the assessor now holds office hours at the center, to be posted on the COA website, after an elevator mishap at the Ritter building.

why_it_matters: The expansion study and shower would go through the town's capital request process, so any cost would compete for capital funds and could end up before residents as a budget item.

The subcommittee's review of the board's policies and procedures will shape how the senior center's governing board is run, including term limits and adjunct members, before any change reaches a vote.
watch_next: Council priorities for the FY28 budget are due on the next Council on Aging agenda.
The chair is to find out who has authority over building use and fees, and the topic stays on the agenda.
